A private, read-only personal reference wiki built with Quartz, published through Cloudflare Workers and protected by Cloudflare Access.

## Overview

Wiki is a private, read-only personal reference site at
`wiki.rjmlaird.co.uk`.

It uses Quartz v4 to turn selected Markdown notes into a searchable
static website. A Cloudflare Worker serves the output, while Cloudflare
Access controls who can view it.

The repository is also private.

These are separate protections: Cloudflare Access protects the website,
not the Git repository or copies of its contents.

### Intended users

- The owner reading and maintaining personal reference material.
- Approved maintainers working on the publishing infrastructure.

The supplied setup specifies an Access policy for the owner's identity
only. Broader access is not part of the documented baseline.

### Scope

The supplied README establishes:

- Markdown source notes.
- Explicit opt-in publication.
- Quartz-generated static output.
- Search and graph data.
- A Worker health route.
- Access-gated delivery.
- Privacy checks.
- CI and deployment workflows.
- Optional copying from an Obsidian publishing folder.

### Read-only meaning

The published website is described as read-only.

Authoring takes place in the repository or an optional local Obsidian
workflow, not through a documented browser editing interface.

### Verification status

This record is based on the supplied README.

Repository privacy, deployed Access policies, alternate-hostname
restrictions and privacy-test results have not been independently
verified for this record.

## Private surfaces

| Surface | Destination | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wiki | <https://wiki.rjmlaird.co.uk> | Private reference website |
| Repository | <https://github.com/rjmlaird/rjmlaird-wiki> | Private source and note history |
| Local preview | `http://localhost:8080` | Local build preview |
| Health route | `/api/health` | Worker health response |

Do not assume that the health route is publicly reachable. Verify how
the Access application covers the hostname and paths.

Do not add the private wiki to public catalogues without a deliberate
decision about what information should be disclosed.

## Architecture

### Layers

| Layer | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `content/` | Markdown source notes |
| Quartz | Static-site generation |
| `public/` | Generated website output |
| `src/index.ts` | Worker health route and static asset delivery |
| Cloudflare Access | Website access decisions |
| GitHub Actions | Checks and deployment |

### Publishing flow

```text
Curated Markdown notes
          ↓
ExplicitPublish filter
          ↓
Quartz build
          ↓
Generated public/ directory
          ↓
Privacy checks
          ↓
Cloudflare Worker deployment
          ↓
Cloudflare Access
          ↓
Approved reader
```

### Repository boundary

All committed content remains subject to repository permissions,
regardless of whether Quartz publishes it.

A note excluded from the website may still exist in:

- Git history.
- Local clones.
- Branches.
- Pull requests.
- Build inputs.
- Backups.

Do not use publication filtering as permission to commit prohibited
sensitive material.

## Content organisation

### Source directory

Notes are maintained under:

```text
content/
```

The README describes organisation by Wheel of Life areas:

```text
01–11
99-Reference
```

Do not invent area names or change their meanings without reviewing
the controlled vocabulary.

### Vocabulary

Use that source when setting classification metadata.

The README requires each page to carry:

```text

sub-area

sensitivity

updated

```

Check the existing content and validation implementation for exact
types and permitted values.

### Explicit publication

A note is eligible for publication only when its frontmatter contains:

```yaml
publish: true
```

The README identifies the Quartz filter as:

```text
ExplicitPublish
```

configured in:


Do not replace this with an implicit publish-everything rule.

### Classification is not access control

Fields such as `sensitivity`, `status` and `review` support organisation
and review.

The supplied README does not establish separate access permissions for
each classification.

Do not assume a sensitive published note is hidden from other authorised
readers merely because its metadata says it is sensitive.

### Updates and review

Keep note-level review metadata distinct from this documentation record's

### Prohibited material

The README explicitly prohibits committing:

- Passwords.
- API keys.
- Recovery codes.
- Account numbers.
- Identity documents.
- Medical records.
- Financial statements.

This restriction applies even when the repository and website are private.

### Placeholders

Use placeholders where a reference needs structure without storing the

For example:

Do not replace placeholders with sensitive values merely to make a note
feel complete.

### Publication review

Before setting `publish: true`, review:

- The note body.
- Frontmatter.
- Links.
- Embedded files.
- Images.
- Attachment metadata.
- Related notes.
- Information exposed through search and graph data.

Do not assume that a note is safe because its title is innocuous.

Central GitHub sign-in and shared application sessions for the RJM Laird ecosystem.

## Overview

Auth provides central sign-in for applications in the RJM Laird ecosystem.

Users sign in with GitHub through `auth.rjmlaird.co.uk`. The service
creates an application session and sets a cookie shared across
`rjmlaird.co.uk` and its subdomains.

Participating applications can then ask the service who the visitor is
without implementing their own GitHub OAuth flow.

Access is restricted to configured GitHub usernames. The service supports
two application roles: `admin` and `user`.

### Intended users

- Approved users signing in to participating applications.
- Developers integrating application-level authentication.
- Maintainers managing access, deployment and operational security.

### Scope

The implementation described by the repository README includes:

- GitHub OAuth sign-in.
- Username-based access lists.
- Shared session cookies.
- Session storage in Workers KV.
- Session lookup.
- Sign-out.
- An account page.
- A liveness endpoint.
- A client package for Worker integrations.
- Hono authentication middleware.

This record is based on the supplied README. The deployed configuration,
source implementation and test results still require maintainer review.

### Authentication and authorisation

A successful sign-in establishes an identity and an assigned role.

Each consuming application remains responsible for deciding what that
identity is permitted to do.

Do not treat the presence of a session as sufficient permission for every
operation. Enforce the relevant role and resource-level rules on the server.

## Live surfaces

| Surface | Destination | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account page | <https://auth.rjmlaird.co.uk> | Current sign-in state |
| Repository | <https://github.com/rjmlaird/rjmlaird-auth> | Implementation and development history |
| Documentation | <https://docs.rjmlaird.co.uk> | Integration and maintainer guidance |
| Client package | `@rjmlaird/auth-client` | Session lookup and integration helpers |

The client source is described as residing in `packages/client`.

Package publication and distribution should be verified before adding
an installation instruction to a consuming repository.

## Architecture

### Components

| Component | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Cloudflare Worker | Hosts the authentication service |
| Hono | Application routing |
| GitHub OAuth | External identity-provider flow |
| Workers KV | Session and OAuth-state storage |
| Shared cookie | Carries the opaque session token |
| Client package | Session lookup and integration helpers |
| Hono middleware | Authentication and role enforcement for consumers |

### Sign-in flow

```text
Browser opens a participating application
                    ↓
Application finds no valid session
                    ↓
Browser redirects to auth /login?redirect=…
                    ↓
GitHub OAuth sign-in
                    ↓
GitHub login checked against configured access lists
                    ↓
Session stored in KV
                    ↓
Shared session cookie set
                    ↓
Browser returns to the validated destination
```

### Session lookup flow

```text
Browser sends shared cookie to an application
                    ↓
Application Worker passes the session cookie to Auth
                    ↓
Auth looks up the session
                    ↓
Application receives the identity and role
                    ↓
Application applies its authorisation rules
```

A Worker service binding is the recommended integration path described
by the README. Without a binding, the client uses the public session
endpoint.

### Trust boundary

The session cookie is shared across the parent domain and its subdomains.

Every application hosted within that cookie boundary must therefore be
treated as part of the authentication trust boundary.

Do not host untrusted applications or third-party-controlled content on
a subdomain that participates in this shared-cookie arrangement.

## Session model

### Cookie

The README specifies:

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Name | `__Secure-rjm_session` |
| Domain | `.rjmlaird.co.uk` |
| HttpOnly | Enabled |
| Secure | Enabled |

### Session storage

Session cookie values are described as random 256-bit tokens.

KV session keys use the SHA-256 hash of the token:

```text
auth:v1:session:<hash>
```

This means the KV key does not contain the usable session token itself.

The exact stored session fields, expiry implementation and any renewal
behaviour should be checked against the source before documenting them
as a stable contract.

### OAuth state

OAuth state is described as:

- Single-use.
- Stored in KV.
- Retained for ten minutes.
- Bound to the initiating browser using a `__Host-` cookie.

State keys use:

```text
auth:v1:state:<state>
```

Do not remove state validation or browser binding to bypass a callback
error.

### Consistency

Workers KV is eventually consistent.

Session creation, lookup and deletion may therefore be affected by
propagation between locations.

The README notes that a newly created session may take approximately
a minute to become visible elsewhere. Treat this as an implementation
consideration, not a guaranteed maximum delay.

Review the deployed behaviour before relying on immediate cross-location
session availability or revocation.

The README identifies Durable Objects or D1 as possible future
alternatives if session consistency becomes a practical problem.

### Add a service binding

In the consuming Worker's `wrangler.toml`:

### Use the client

```ts
import {
  getSession,
  loginUrl,
} from "@rjmlaird/auth-client";

export default {
  async fetch(
    request: Request,
    env: { AUTH: Fetcher },
  ) {
    const session = await getSession(request, {
      binding: env.AUTH,
    });

    if (!session) {
      return Response.redirect(loginUrl(request.url), 302);
    }

    return new Response(
      `Hello ${session.name ?? session.login}`,
    );
  },
};
```

This example follows the README's Worker integration.

required Cloudflare runtime types.

are handled appropriately.

- Redirects.
- The actual response status.

- Localhost is allowed in the development configuration.
- Local cookie handling matches the implementation.

Check:

- The binding name is `AUTH`.
- The target service is `rjmlaird-auth`.

- The target environment is correct.

Overview

Auth provides central sign-in for applications in the RJM Laird ecosystem.

Users sign in with GitHub through auth.rjmlaird.co.uk. The service creates an application session and sets a cookie shared across rjmlaird.co.uk and its subdomains.

Participating applications can then ask the service who the visitor is without implementing their own GitHub OAuth flow.

Access is restricted to configured GitHub usernames. The service supports two application roles: admin and user.

Intended users

  • Approved users signing in to participating applications.
  • Developers integrating application-level authentication.
  • Maintainers managing access, deployment and operational security.

Scope

The implementation described by the repository README includes:

  • GitHub OAuth sign-in.
  • Username-based access lists.
  • Shared session cookies.
  • Session storage in Workers KV.
  • Session lookup.
  • Sign-out.
  • An account page.
  • A liveness endpoint.
  • A client package for Worker integrations.
  • Hono authentication middleware.

This record is based on the supplied README. The deployed configuration, source implementation and test results still require maintainer review.

Authentication and authorisation

A successful sign-in establishes an identity and an assigned role.

Each consuming application remains responsible for deciding what that identity is permitted to do.

Do not treat the presence of a session as sufficient permission for every operation. Enforce the relevant role and resource-level rules on the server.

Add a service binding

The README recommends this path to avoid routing session lookups through the public hostname.

Use the client

import {
  getSession,
  loginUrl,
} from "@rjmlaird/auth-client";

export default {
  async fetch(
    request: Request,
    env: { AUTH: Fetcher },
  ) {
    const session = await getSession(request, {
      binding: env.AUTH,
    });

    if (!session) {
      return Response.redirect(loginUrl(request.url), 302);
    }

    return new Response(
      `Hello ${session.name ?? session.login}`,
    );
  },
};

This example follows the README’s Worker integration.

Ensure the consuming project’s TypeScript configuration includes the required Cloudflare runtime types.

Security considerations

Shared-subdomain trust

The shared session cookie makes participating subdomains part of a common trust boundary.

Review new subdomains and third-party hosting arrangements before placing them beneath that boundary.

Cookie handling

Do not log session cookie values.

Preserve the intended security attributes when setting or clearing the cookie.

Check that sign-out clears the same cookie scope used during sign-in.

Session responses

Keep session responses out of shared caches.

Do not persist authenticated identity responses in public build output, static files or logs.

OAuth state

Preserve state validation, expiry and browser binding.

Because state is stored in KV, review whether the implementation provides the required single-use behaviour under concurrent requests and cross-location access. A stated single-use intent should be checked against the storage and validation logic.

Access changes

Establish how access-list changes affect existing sessions.

The README does not describe a completed revoke-all-sessions capability.

Do not assume that removing a username from configuration immediately revokes every active session.

Rate limiting

Asset upload, image processing, public CDN delivery and an Access-protected digital asset manager with an offline mirror.

## Overview

CDN and DAM combines asset ingestion, image processing, public asset
delivery and a digital asset management interface in one repository.

The system is organised around four components:

- An authenticated upload Worker.
- A queue-driven image processor.
- A digital asset management API and browser.
- A local synchronisation and offline browsing tool.

The CDN delivery surface remains public. Cloudflare Access protects the
DAM interface and API, not the public CDN objects.

### Intended users

- Maintainers uploading and inspecting assets.
- Developers integrating published assets into websites and applications.
- Approved users browsing the DAM.
- Operators maintaining a local offline copy.

### Documentation status

This record is based on the supplied README, Access setup instructions
and root package configuration.

The supplied README states that the rebuilt stack was not tested against
a real Cloudflare account at the time it was prepared. It reports type
and JavaScript syntax checks, not a verified production deployment.

Treat deployment, bindings, Access policies and end-to-end processing as
requiring maintainer verification.

The project-level `active` status does not establish that the reconstructed
pipeline has been validated in production.

## Reconstruction history

### Upload Worker

`cdn-upload` is described as a TypeScript reconstruction of a previously
deployed bundle.

The README states that it preserves the original:

- Routes.
- Object-key layout.
- Query parameters.
- Response behaviour.

One deliberate ordering change was introduced: the metadata record is
written before the original object is uploaded to R2.

### Metadata ordering

The R2 write triggers the processing event.

Writing metadata after the object could allow the processor to finish
and mark the asset ready, only for the upload Worker to overwrite that
state with an earlier processing status.

The reconstructed ordering is:

```text
Write initial metadata
          ↓
Write original object to R2
          ↓
R2 event triggers processing
          ↓
Processor writes renditions and ready metadata
```

This addresses the race described in the README. Upload failures,
repeated events and concurrent replacement behaviour still require
end-to-end validation.

### Processor

`cdn-processor` is new code, not a reconstruction from the supplied
deployed upload bundle.

Before deploying it, inspect any existing deployed Worker with that
name and compare:

- Its code or available deployment history.
- Bindings.
- Queue configuration.
- Image processing behaviour.
- Metadata format.
- Object-key layout.

Do not overwrite an existing processor solely because the reconstructed
repository includes one.

### Scripts

The setup and upload scripts are described as rewrites of the earlier
README's helpers.

Inspect them before execution. Do not assume a helper is safe or
non-destructive solely because it is named `setup.sh`.

## Architecture

### Upload and processing flow

```text
Authenticated upload
          ↓
cdn-upload writes KV metadata
          ↓
Original object stored in R2
          ↓
R2 event notification and queue
          ↓
cdn-processor
          ↓
Cloudflare Images transformation
          ↓
Thumbnail and web rendition stored in R2
          ↓
KV metadata updated to ready
```

The event notification, queue and consumer bindings must be confirmed
in the actual Cloudflare configuration.

### DAM flow

```text
Approved browser or service client
          ↓
Cloudflare Access
          ↓
dam-api
          ↓
Manifest and asset browsing interface
```

The supplied implementation delegates authentication to Cloudflare Access.

No authentication logic is described inside `dam-api` itself.

### Offline flow

```text
dam-sync with Access service credentials
          ↓
Remote manifest and asset retrieval
          ↓
Local files and local manifest
          ↓
Loopback-only offline browser
```

Verify how credentials are applied to every protected asset request,
not only the manifest request.

## Storage and object layout

### Originals

The upload example uses:

```text
media/originals/photo.jpg
```

Confirm the complete key layout for all supported asset types against
the upload implementation.

### Image renditions

Image renditions are written beneath:

```text
media/renditions/<path-without-extension>/
├── thumb.webp
└── web.webp
```

For nested uploads, the path is preserved rather than using only the
basename.

This avoids collisions caused solely by two files with the same basename
in different directories.

It does not, by itself, establish how files with the same path stem but
different extensions are handled. Check that case before relying on
replacement or uniqueness behaviour.

### Metadata

The reconstructed implementation assumes that `CDN_METADATA` is a
Workers KV binding.

The README identifies uncertainty in the earlier setup over whether
that name referred to KV or an R2 bucket.

Resolve this before deployment.

The metadata's `renditions` field is described as containing R2 object
keys, not necessarily complete public URLs.

### Manifest

The DAM exposes:

```text
GET /api/manifest
```

A legacy `manifest.json` object at the public CDN root is described as
unused by this implementation.

Do not delete it until checking for consumers outside this repository.

## Access model

### Public CDN

Reads at:

```text
[https://cdn.rjmlaird.co.uk](https://cdn.rjmlaird.co.uk)
```

remain unauthenticated.

Assets intended to remain confidential must not be published through
that public delivery surface.

Protecting the DAM does not make the underlying public CDN assets private.

### Upload and reprocessing

The upload Worker uses:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The reprocessing route also uses the configured token.

Do not place this token in browser-delivered application code, public
examples or committed configuration.

### DAM access

The DAM browser and API are intended to sit behind Cloudflare Access.

Treat Access configuration as a deployment prerequisite, not an optional
interface enhancement.

Check alternate Worker hostnames and routes to ensure they do not expose
an unintended path around the protected hostname.

### Relationship to rjmlaird-auth

This implementation uses Cloudflare Access for DAM access.

It is not documented as using the shared application sessions supplied
by `rjmlaird-auth`.

Do not replace or bypass Access without reviewing both browser and
service-client requirements.

### Synchronise

From `dam-sync`:

The README describes an incremental synchronisation process using SHA-256
comparison.

It retrieves:

- Documents.
- Media originals.
- Ready renditions.

Verify the exact manifest and comparison behaviour before documenting
stronger integrity or recovery guarantees.

### Browse locally

```bash
node dam-sync.js serve
```

The documented destination is:

```text
http://localhost:8787
```

The server binds to:

```text
127.0.0.1
```

The local manifest is described as having the same shape as the remote

status.

### Deletion behaviour

Remote deletions are not propagated to the local folder.

The sync process does not delete local files.

Consequences include:

- Previously downloaded files may remain after remote deletion.
- Local storage usage can grow.
- A mirror may contain historical files.
- Remote removal is not a device-erasure mechanism.

Do not describe this as an exact destructive mirror.

### Local protection

The offline copy contains actual asset files.

Use appropriate device security and access controls. Do not expose the
local server to the wider network without a separate security review.

Keep the local server and development stack on distinct ports when
running them simultaneously.

### Ownership

Ryan Laird owns asset-publication and access decisions.

Maintainers are responsible for preserving upload compatibility,
processing behaviour, metadata integrity and recoverability.

### Routine checks

Review:

- Upload success.
- Processing failures and queue behaviour.
- Metadata status.
- Rendition availability.
- DAM Access enforcement.
- Public delivery.
- Offline synchronisation.
- Storage consumption.
- Service-token expiry and ownership.
- Dependency and runtime support.

### Data consistency

Look for:

- Metadata without an original object.
- Originals without metadata.
- Ready records with missing renditions.
- Renditions not referenced by metadata.
- Replaced originals with stale renditions.
- Failed processing left in an intermediate state.

Establish repair procedures before running bulk corrective operations.

### Backup and recovery

Identify the authoritative copies of:

- Original assets.
- Metadata.
- Renditions.
- Access configuration.
- Resource bindings.
- Deployment configuration.

The offline copy can support recovery, but it is not automatically a
complete backup strategy.

Verify:

- Sync completion.
- Available disk capacity.
- Protection from accidental local deletion.
- Whether historical versions exist.
- Whether remote metadata can be reconstructed.
- Whether originals can be restored safely.
- Whether renditions can be regenerated.

### Incident response

For a pipeline failure:

1. Identify whether upload, events, processing, metadata or delivery is affected.
2. Preserve diagnostic information.
3. Prevent further corruption where necessary.
4. Restore a compatible service state.
5. Repair affected assets using a reviewed process.
6. Verify the manifest and public delivery.
7. Record the cause and preventive changes.

For unintended public disclosure, consider every surface:

- Public CDN.
- DAM.
- Downloaded copies.
- Caches.
- Offline mirrors.

Removing an item from the DAM interface alone does not remove those copies.

## Troubleshooting

These checks are diagnostic starting points. The supplied README does
not establish production-tested recovery procedures.

### Upload returns an authentication error

Check:

- The bearer header.
- The target environment.
- The configured `CDN_API_TOKEN`.
- Whether the token was rotated.
- Whether scripts still use an older value.

Do not place the token in a query string.

### An asset remains in processing

Check:

- The original exists.
- Initial metadata was written.
- R2 event notifications target the intended queue.
- The processor consumes that queue.
- The Images binding is available.
- Processor logs show successful output.
- Metadata is updated after processing.

For local development, remember that manual reprocessing is required
by the documented workflow.

### Ready metadata exists but previews fail

Check:

- Rendition keys in metadata.
- Actual R2 objects.
- URL construction.
- CDN-origin configuration.
- `/files/*` behaviour.
- Access credentials.
- Cached responses.

Do not assume that a ready status proves every referenced object exists.

### The DAM is unexpectedly public

Check:

- The Access application hostname.
- Policy configuration.
- Alternate Worker routes and hostnames.
- Whether the request is bypassing the protected surface.

Treat missing Access enforcement as a security issue, not merely a
navigation problem.

### dam-sync receives a login page

Check:

- The Access service-token headers.
- Client ID and secret.
- Token expiry or revocation.
- The Service Auth policy.
- The configured DAM base URL.

Inspect response status and content type before treating the response
as a manifest.

### Offline files remain after remote deletion

This is the documented non-deleting sync behaviour.

Do not add a bulk-delete workaround without a reviewed retention and
reconciliation policy.

### Images processing fails locally

Check:

- Cloudflare authentication.
- Images binding configuration.
- The actual processor port.
- The test asset type.
- Whether a remote test environment is required.

### Deployment changes existing bindings

Compare the proposed `wrangler.toml` bindings with the currently deployed
Worker before redeploying.

Restore the intended configuration deliberately. Do not guess resource
types or identifiers.

Overview

CDN and DAM combines asset ingestion, image processing, public asset delivery and a digital asset management interface in one repository.

The system is organised around four components:

  • An authenticated upload Worker.
  • A queue-driven image processor.
  • A digital asset management API and browser.
  • A local synchronisation and offline browsing tool.

The CDN delivery surface remains public. Cloudflare Access protects the DAM interface and API, not the public CDN objects.

Intended users

  • Maintainers uploading and inspecting assets.
  • Developers integrating published assets into websites and applications.
  • Approved users browsing the DAM.
  • Operators maintaining a local offline copy.

Reconstruction history

Upload Worker

cdn-upload is described as a TypeScript reconstruction of a previously deployed bundle.

The README states that it preserves the original:

  • Routes.
  • Object-key layout.
  • Query parameters.
  • Response behaviour.

One deliberate ordering change was introduced: the metadata record is written before the original object is uploaded to R2.

Metadata ordering

The R2 write triggers the processing event.

Writing metadata after the object could allow the processor to finish and mark the asset ready, only for the upload Worker to overwrite that state with an earlier processing status.

The reconstructed ordering is:

Write initial metadata
          ↓
Write original object to R2
          ↓
R2 event triggers processing
          ↓
Processor writes renditions and ready metadata

This addresses the race described in the README. Upload failures, repeated events and concurrent replacement behaviour still require end-to-end validation.

Processor

cdn-processor is new code, not a reconstruction from the supplied deployed upload bundle.

Before deploying it, inspect any existing deployed Worker with that name and compare:

  • Its code or available deployment history.
  • Bindings.
  • Queue configuration.
  • Image processing behaviour.
  • Metadata format.
  • Object-key layout.

Do not overwrite an existing processor solely because the reconstructed repository includes one.

Scripts

The setup and upload scripts are described as rewrites of the earlier README’s helpers.

Inspect them before execution. Do not assume a helper is safe or non-destructive solely because it is named setup.sh.

### Current baseline

### Safe publication boundary

Before exposing a tool through an unauthenticated endpoint, review:

- The information it can read.
- The actions it can perform.
- The resources it can consume.
- The credentials it can exercise.

Public availability of the documentation does not justify public access
to private capabilities.

- Auditability.

protect the server operation.

## Troubleshooting

These are diagnostic starting points, not a record of tested incidents.

### The client cannot connect

Check:

- The exact endpoint, including `/mcp`.
- Local versus deployed destination.
- Worker availability.
- HTTPS configuration for production.
- Client transport support.
- Proxy configuration.
- Network or access restrictions.

Inspect protocol and client errors rather than assuming the URL should
render a web page.

### The client connects but shows no tools

Check:

- Tool registration executes.
- The expected source revision is deployed.
- The SDK API matches the installed version.
- Initialisation succeeds.
- The client has refreshed its tool inventory.
- The endpoint is the intended server.

### A tool rejects valid-looking arguments

Compare the client arguments with the server's actual schema.

Check:

- Required fields.
- Types.
- Enumerated values.
- Bounds.
- Optional and null behaviour.
- Schema changes since the client connected.

Do not weaken validation simply to accept an incorrect call.

### An upstream request fails

Check:

- Destination.
- Credentials.
- Binding configuration.
- Request format.
- Service permissions.
- Timeout behaviour.
- Upstream response.

Distinguish authentication failures, invalid requests and temporary
service failures in the returned error.

### Claude Desktop does not load the configuration

Check:

- The current configuration location.
- Valid JSON syntax.
- Existing server entries.
- Availability of `npx`.
- Proxy-package resolution.
- Endpoint accuracy.
- Client restart or reconnect requirements.

Do not include comments inside strict JSON.

### Binding types are out of date

After changing `wrangler.jsonc`, run:

```bash
npx wrangler types
```

Then run the repository's available checks.

Also verify the runtime binding. Correct generated types do not create
the remote resource.

### Worker error 1102 occurs

The repository guidance identifies error 1102 as a CPU or memory limit
issue.

Retrieve the current Worker limits and error documentation before
diagnosing it.

Inspect the tool's workload and resource usage. Do not assume a fixed
limit or that retrying will resolve an excessive operation.

Interactive historical and projected UK climate visualization tool featuring warming stripes, Met Office regional observation series, and CMIP6 climate model projections.

# Local Climate Time Machine

Drag a slider through 140+ years of measured UK weather and a model-based view of the next 25, for a chosen region, with plain-English notes on what changed.

The slider track is the region's own **warming stripes**: one bar per year, coloured by how far that year sits from the 1961–1990 average. Years beyond the last measurement are hatched.

## Quick start

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # first run downloads the data automatically
```

`npm run fetch-data` re-downloads everything. `npm test` checks the parser and bias-adjustment logic. `npm run build` makes a static site in `dist/` that can be hosted under any path.

## Real data sources

| What | Source | Licence |
|---|---|---|
| Observed temperature (mean, max, min), rainfall (annual, winter, summer) and days of air frost (from 1961) | Met Office UK regional series, derived from HadUK-Grid | Open Government Licence v3.0 |
| Projections to 2050 | 7 CMIP6 HighResMIP models via the Open-Meteo Climate API | CC BY 4.0 (check their terms if your use is commercial) |

Nothing is bundled or hand-typed: `scripts/fetch-data.mjs` downloads both sources and writes `public/data/*.json`.

## What the app shows

- **Time slider** over the stripes, with play/pause and clickable markers for notable UK events.
- **Four charts**: temperature (mean, summer, daytime highs, night-time lows), rainfall (annual, winter, summer), air frost days, and growing-season dryness, with each year, a 10-year average, the model mean and the model range.
- **Annotation panel** whose sentences are computed from the data (rank, anomaly, how often a 2022-style summer occurs in the models), plus short curated notes on well-documented UK events.

## Honest limitations

- **Frost days** are measured only from 1961, and model frost counts are biased, so only their change is used.
- **Region, not county.** The Midlands series is the closest published match to Leicestershire.
- **One emissions pathway.** The HighResMIP models are run under SSP5-8.5, so there is no low/medium selector yet.
- **Projections stop at 2050.**
- **Dryness is simplified**: standardised April–September rainfall, not SPEI.
- Models are sampled at one point per region and bias-adjusted by delta change. See `docs/methods.md`.

## Roadmap

1. Multi-scenario projections (low/medium/high) from UKCP18 via CEDA, which needs a free account.
2. Finer geographies using HadUK-Grid area averages.
3. Seasonal views and region comparison.
4. Proper SPEI with an evaporation estimate.

## Structure

```
scripts/        fetch-data.mjs + lib/ (Met Office parser, model processing)
test/           parser and adjustment tests
src/lib/        data lookups, narrative sentences, curated events
src/components/ StripeSlider, ClimateChart, AnnotationPanel, Method
docs/           data-sources.md, methods.md
```

# Data sources

## Observations: Met Office UK regional series
- Files: `https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/pub/data/weather/uk/climate/datasets/{Tmean|Rainfall}/date/{Region}.txt`
- Browse and download manually: https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/research/climate/maps-and-data/uk-and-regional-series
- Derived from HadUK-Grid: station data interpolated to a 1 km grid, then averaged over regions.
- Series: `Tmean`, `Tmax`, `Tmin`, `Rainfall`, `AirFrost`. The last three are optional; if one fails to download, that variable is left out.
- Columns used: monthly values (for April–September rainfall), summer (JJA) mean temperature, annual mean temperature, annual rainfall.
- Licence: Open Government Licence v3.0. Credit the Met Office.
- Region file names are set in `scripts/fetch-data.mjs`. If the Met Office renames one, the script skips that region and warns.

## Projections: Open-Meteo Climate API
- Endpoint: `https://climate-api.open-meteo.com/v1/climate`
- Models: MRI_AGCM3_2_S, EC_Earth3P_HR, NICAM16_8S, CMCC_CM2_VHR4, FGOALS_f3_H, HiRAM_SIT_HR, MPI_ESM1_2_XR (CMIP6 HighResMIP).
- Variables: daily mean, maximum and minimum temperature and precipitation, 1991 to 2050.
- Licence: CC BY 4.0, free for non-commercial use. Commercial use needs their API plan.

## For multi-scenario work
UKCP18 projections (RCP2.6, 4.5, 8.5 and the 12 km local set) are the standard UK source. They are on the CEDA archive and need a free account, so the fetch script does not use them yet.


# Methods

## Reference period
Anomalies and the dryness index use 1961–1990. Bias adjustment uses 1991–2020, the current 30-year climate normal.

## Observed series
`buildObservations` joins temperature and rainfall by year. Growing-season rainfall is the sum of April to September monthly totals, and is null if any month is missing.

## Model processing
1. Daily model output is aggregated to annual mean temperature, summer (Jun–Aug) mean temperature, annual rainfall and April–September rainfall. Years with missing days are dropped.
2. Rainfall totals are scaled to a 365.25-day year so models with 360-day calendars compare fairly.
3. Frost days are days with minimum temperature below 0 °C, scaled to a 365.25-day year. Winter rainfall is December to February, labelled by the year of its January (1991 is dropped from model baselines because December 1990 isn't requested). Summer is June to August.
4. **Delta-change adjustment** per model: temperature = observed 1991–2020 mean + (model value − model 1991–2020 mean); rainfall (annual, seasonal) = observed 1991–2020 mean × (model value ÷ model 1991–2020 mean). Temperatures and frost days use the difference; frost days are floored at zero. This keeps the regional observed climate and uses the model only for change.
5. Only years after the last observed year are kept as projections.

## Dryness index
`dry = −(AprSepRain − mean₁₉₆₁₋₁₉₉₀) / sd₁₉₆₁₋₁₉₉₀`. Positive means drier than the reference. It has no evaporation term, so it understates drying in warmer years.

## Narrative sentences
Computed in `src/lib/narrative.js`: anomalies, ranks, and the share of model-years in a ±5-year window that exceed a threshold (summer 2022, or the 90th percentile of 1991–2020 annual temperature). Because the window pools model-years, the shares describe the ensemble, not a probability forecast.

## Uncertainty
The shaded band is the min–max across models and years. It mixes model disagreement with year-to-year variability and is not a confidence interval. All models share one emissions pathway, so scenario uncertainty is not shown.

designated-habitat boundaries**, and **live river/water data** — defaults to
Leicester & Leicestershire, but works anywhere in England (Wales/Scotland/NI
are not covered by the layers used here — see caveats below). Open
`index.html` in a browser, no setup, no API keys.

## What's in it

**Vegetation health (NDVI)** — Copernicus Global Land Service, served free
by VITO with no key: `globalland.vito.be/wmts`, layer
`clms_global_ndvi_1km_v2_10daily`. 1 km resolution, 10-daily composites —
coarse, but enough to see landscape-scale greenness across a county the size
of Leicestershire. Darker green = denser/healthier vegetation. Opacity is
adjustable so you can compare it against the basemap or the habitat layers
underneath.

*Caveat worth passing to students*: Copernicus has iterated this product
line (v1 → v2 → v3, 1km and 300m variants), and the newer, higher-resolution
NDVI products have moved toward the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem, which
needs a free account. The 1km v2 layer used here is the version confirmed
still served on the open, no-key VITO endpoint at the time of building —
worth checking [land.copernicus.eu/global](https://land.copernicus.eu/global/)
for whether a newer no-key layer exists before relying on this for
current research.

**Designated habitats** — click "Load habitat layers for this view" to pull
live boundaries for whatever's in view, from Natural England/Defra's open
geospatial services (Open Government Licence, no key):
- National Nature Reserves — confirmed live feed
- Local Nature Reserves — confirmed live feed
- Ancient Woodland Inventory — confirmed live feed
- Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) — **best-effort**: I found
  Natural England's SSSI data is definitely served the same way, but
  couldn't confirm the exact service name before building this. If the SSSI
  chip fails silently (a toast will say so), the polygon layer isn't
  reachable at that URL and needs updating — see "Fixing a broken layer"
  below.

Click any shaded polygon for a popup with whatever attribute fields Natural
England publishes for that site (name, designation date, area, etc. — this
varies by layer).

**River & water health** — two live Environment Agency sources, combined:
- **River level** (`environment.data.gov.uk/flood-monitoring`) — same
  "compared to typical range" approach as the UK Drought Monitor tool
- **Water Quality Archive / WIMS** (`environment.data.gov.uk/water-quality`)
  — nearby sampling points with their most recent determinand readings
  (nitrate, phosphate, dissolved oxygen, ammonia, etc. — whatever's been
  sampled there recently). **This one is also best-effort** — the Water
  Quality Archive API's exact endpoint shape wasn't independently verified
  during a live test before shipping this tool, only documented as existing.
  If it errors, the panel says so and links straight to the archive's own
  browse page rather than pretending to have live numbers.

Leicestershire's main watercourses (River Soar, River Wreake, River Welland,
River Sence) are covered by EA's network, so station search should return
useful results across most of the county.

## Honesty notes (please keep these in mind before presenting results)

This tool follows the same principle as the earlier drought and wildfire
tools in this series: a labelled gap or an honest "couldn't confirm" beats a
confident-looking number that isn't real.

- The **SSSI layer** and the **Water Quality Archive integration** are
  flagged above as best-effort. Everything else (NDVI, NNR, LNR, Ancient
  Woodland, river level) is a confirmed, tested live endpoint.
- NDVI is a **regional greenness signal**, not a biodiversity score — dense
  vegetation isn't automatically "healthy" (a dense stand of an invasive
  species reads the same as ancient woodland). Pair it with the habitat
  layers and use it to prompt discussion, not as a standalone verdict.
- Designated-site boundaries (NNR/LNR/SSSI/Ancient Woodland) mark
  legal/planning status, not real-time ecological condition. Natural England
  publishes separate SSSI *condition* assessments (favourable/unfavourable)
  as a different, non-spatial dataset not wired into this tool.

Reusable lab tool for teaching UK drought risk combining live Copernicus drought indicators with real-time EA and SEPA hydrology data.

## Overview

A reusable lab tool for teaching UK drought risk — combines **live Copernicus
drought indicators** with **live Environment Agency hydrology data**. No API
keys, no setup: open `index.html` in a browser.

### What's live in this tool

**Copernicus European & Global Drought Observatories (EDO/GDO)** — run by the
Joint Research Centre, part of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service:
- **Combined Drought Indicator (CDI)** — the headline Watch/Warning/Alert
  agricultural drought classification
- **SPI (short & long term)** — Standardised Precipitation Index, ERA5-based,
  with a switchable accumulation period (SPI-1/3/6/12/24/48)
- **Soil moisture anomaly**, **Low-flow index**, **Risk of Drought Impact
  (agriculture)**

These are fetched directly from the live public WMS
(`drought.emergency.copernicus.eu/api/wms`) — the same service behind the
official EDO map viewer. SPI, SPI-long-term and Drought Impact Risk are
**queryable**: click anywhere on the map and the tool sends a live
GetFeatureInfo request and shows the value at that point.

**Environment Agency (England) & SEPA (Scotland) real-time hydrology** — click
"Find UK stations near map centre" (or search an English town) and the tool
queries, live and in parallel:
- `environment.data.gov.uk/flood-monitoring` (England) — river level stations
  compared against each station's own published *typical range* (95th/5th
  percentile band), plus rainfall gauges with a live-computed 24-hour total
- `timeseries.sepa.org.uk/KiWIS` (Scotland) — SEPA's Time Series Data Service,
  river level stations compared against each station's published *median
  annual maximum/minimum level* (the closest published equivalent to EA's
  typical range)

Both are free, open, no API key required.

**Wales (Natural Resources Wales) and Northern Ireland (DfI Rivers)** — these
are *not* wired in as live feeds, for two different honest reasons:
- NRW's River Levels API requires a free personal subscription key
  (sign up at [api-portal.naturalresources.wales](https://api-portal.naturalresources.wales/))
  — the tool doesn't embed a shared key, since that's tied to an individual
  account. The endpoint pattern is
  `https://api.naturalresources.wales/rivers-and-seas/v1/api/StationData/historical?location={id}&parameter={id}`
  (header `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key`) if you want to extend the tool with
  your own key — you'd also need to resolve station IDs first, which isn't
  confirmed as a no-key operation.
- DfI Rivers (Northern Ireland) doesn't publish a public API at all — only a
  web viewer.

Instead, the results panel always includes direct links to NRW's and DfI's
official live viewers, clearly labelled, so nothing is silently missing.

### What's NOT live — reservoir stocks

There is no open, live UK reservoir-stock API. The Environment Agency
publishes reservoir levels once a month, as part of the
[Water Situation national report](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/water-situation-national-monthly-reports-for-england-2026)
(PDF/CSV). The "Reservoir stocks" panel is a manual entry table for exactly
this reason — type in each region's % figure from the latest report and the
bars update. It's a deliberate design choice: better an honest manual field
than a fabricated live number.

### Using it in a session

1. Pick a drought indicator from the chips above the map.
2. Use "Jump to latest indicator date" (omits the date parameter — per
   Copernicus's own documentation this returns whichever date is most
   recently available) or step back/forward in 10-day increments to look at
   how conditions evolved.
3. For SPI layers, switch the accumulation period (SPI-1 vs SPI-12 tells very
   different stories — short-term dryness vs multi-year reservoir/groundwater
   deficit) — a good discussion point in itself.
4. Click the map on a queryable layer for the point value.
5. Search a town or pan the map and pull live EA station data to ground-truth
   the satellite/model-based indicators against actual river and rainfall
   readings.
6. Enter the latest monthly reservoir figures for a fuller regional picture.

### Attribution (built in, but worth knowing)

- Drought indicators: © European Commission / Joint Research Centre,
  Copernicus European & Global Drought Observatories
- Hydrology data: Environment Agency, Open Government Licence v3.0
- Basemap: © CARTO, © OpenStreetMap contributors

### Extending it

The `LAYERS` array near the top of the script is the whole indicator
catalogue — add another EDO WMS layer name from the
[capabilities document](https://drought.emergency.copernicus.eu/api/wms?REQUEST=GetCapabilities&SERVICE=WMS&VERSION=1.1.1)
and it appears as a new toggle automatically. Station search radius, default
map view, and the reservoir region list are all plain variables near the
top of their respective sections.

Interactive educational simulation and lab exploring seismic wave propagation, P-S wave travel-time distance, magnitude scales, and earthquake physics.

## Plan and Architecture

**Astro + vanilla TypeScript** (recommended over Next.js): static-first, ships near-zero JavaScript except one script on the lab page, cheap to host, and matches the Astro stack used across the repository ecosystem.

```
src/
  lib/sim-core.ts        pure physics (tested) → wave propagation and travel-time core
  data/                  site.ts, labs.ts (registry), earthquakes.ts (config + copy)
  layouts/               Base.astro (SEO), LabLayout.astro (reusable lab template)
  components/            ModuleDocs.astro (method/equations/assumptions/limitations/try this)
  pages/                 /, /labs, /labs/earthquakes, /about, /contact, /privacy, 404, sitemap.xml
  scripts/earthquakes.ts client interactivity for the lab only
  styles/global.css      tokens, focus states, reduced motion
public/                  robots.txt, favicon.svg (add og.png, 1200×630)
tests/unit, tests/a11y   Vitest unit tests; built-HTML accessibility smoke test

```

## Setup & Commands

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # http://localhost:4321
npm test             # unit tests (P–S distance, magnitude, wave velocity)
npm run check        # Astro/TypeScript check
npm run build        # outputs dist/
npm run test:a11y    # builds, then smoke-tests dist/ HTML
npm run format       # Prettier

```

No environment variables are required for deployment or local execution.

## Deploy (Cloudflare Pages, Vercel or Netlify)

Build command `npm run build`, output directory `dist`, Node 20+. Point `labs.rjmlaird.co.uk` at the project (CNAME). The `site` URL in `astro.config.mjs` and `src/data/site.ts` drives canonical URLs and the sitemap.

**Checklist:** add `public/og.png` · confirm contact email in `src/data/site.ts` · `npm test && npm run test:a11y` · keyboard-only run through all modules · test at 320 px · check with reduced motion on · verify `/sitemap.xml`, `/robots.txt` and the 404 page · run a screen-reader pass (VoiceOver/NVDA) and a Lighthouse accessibility audit.

## Add a New Lab

1. Add an entry to `src/data/labs.ts` and the route to `site.routes` in `src/data/site.ts`.
2. Put pure calculations in `src/lib/` with tests in `tests/unit/`.
3. Create `src/pages/labs/<slug>.astro` using `LabLayout` (title block, disclaimer, further-reading slot) and `ModuleDocs`.
4. Keep copy and presets in `src/data/<slug>.ts`; put interactivity in `src/scripts/<slug>.ts`.

## Accessibility Checklist (Manual)

Semantic landmarks and one `h1` per page; tabs follow the ARIA tab pattern (arrow keys, Home/End); interface controls are keyboard-navigable; animations feature a pause button and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; wave types and travel-time paths are distinguished by label and line style, not colour alone; live regions announce updates.

## Post-MVP Roadmap

1. Real historical earthquake case studies and advanced seismic scenarios.
2. Fault-type and rupture-direction visualisations.
3. Shake-intensity and local-site-effect expanders.
4. CSV/data export pipelines.
5. Embeddable widget builds.
6. Optional privacy-respecting analytics (update `/privacy` first).
7. Git-based lab workflow (PR template, lab checklist).
8. Community feedback and contribution workflow.

  1. Real historical earthquake case studies and advanced seismic scenarios.
  2. Fault-type and rupture-direction visualisations.
  3. Shake-intensity and local-site-effect expanders.
  4. CSV/data export pipelines.
  5. Embeddable widget builds.
  6. Optional privacy-respecting analytics (update /privacy first).
  7. Git-based lab workflow (PR template, lab checklist).
  8. Community feedback and contribution workflow.

Local-first genealogy research workspace and GEDCOM tree explorer with per-person private notes, hypotheses, and multi-view SVG chart rendering.

# Kinship Notes

Part of [rjmlaird.co.uk apps](https://apps.rjmlaird.co.uk). A local-first genealogy research workspace for **kinship-notes.apps.rjmlaird.co.uk**. Import a GEDCOM, explore the family as a tree, and attach private research notes, questions, tasks and hypotheses to each person. The GEDCOM is never rewritten or uploaded: everything stays in the browser's `localStorage`, and the Worker only serves static assets.

## Views

- **Record & notes**: person details, immediate relatives, and per-person annotations.
- **Family tree**: whole tree (every person, one row per generation), hourglass, pedigree, descendants, and a radial fan chart. Pan/zoom, generation limits, jump-to-person.

## Commands

```sh
pnpm --filter kinship-notes dev        # Vite dev server
pnpm --filter kinship-notes test       # parser and layout tests (vitest)
pnpm --filter kinship-notes typecheck  # app + worker
pnpm --filter kinship-notes build      # tsc + vite build into dist/
pnpm --filter kinship-notes cf:dev     # wrangler dev against dist/
pnpm --filter kinship-notes deploy     # build + wrangler deploy
```

`samples/sample-77-people.ged` is a synthetic tree for trying every view.

## How it works

- `src/gedcom.ts`: level-aware GEDCOM reader. Reconciles one-sided FAMC/FAMS/CHIL links and drops dangling references.
- `src/tree.ts`: pure layout engine (no DOM), covered by `tree.test.ts`.
- `src/TreeView.tsx`: SVG rendering with pan/zoom.
- `src/App.tsx`: import, search, notes. Notes are stored per source filename with a content fingerprint, so a changed file triggers a warning rather than silently re-attaching notes.

## Known limits

- UTF-8 GEDCOM only (ANSEL and UTF-16 files will show garbled names).
- A few thousand people are fine; tens of thousands need viewport culling.
- `localStorage` is about 5 MB per origin; very large files cannot be persisted (the app warns and offers a notes export).
- Notes are device-local. There is no sync.

## Branding

Kinship Notes is the one light-only app. It uses the brand light theme (`<html data-theme="light">`, tokens from `/brand.css`), Space Grotesk and Inter. Female/male colouring uses the violet (category) and teal (primary) roles. See [docs/branding.md](../../docs/branding.md).

The checklist for adding a new service or hostname to the rjmlaird.co.uk estate, from justification to documentation, in a single pull request.

A new service touches DNS, security, monitoring and documentation, so it is added in one reviewed change. Nothing here may be skipped; "not applicable" needs a stated reason.

## Requirements

| # | Requirement | Where it is recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Justify the hostname.** Meet at least one test in [When a subdomain is justified](../platform/governance/subdomains.md#when-a-subdomain-is-justified); otherwise use a path | ADR or pull request description |
| 2 | **Add a catalogue entry** to `data/subdomains.json` | [Subdomain catalogue](../platform/governance/subdomains.md) |
| 3 | **Write a first-party service page** with one responsibility and its boundaries | `docs/catalogue/first-party/<slug>.md` |
| 4 | **Set visibility and lifecycle explicitly.** Default to restricted for anything that writes, integrates or manages | Catalogue and page front matter |
| 5 | **Decide ownership.** Name who maintains it and where the code lives | Service page |
| 6 | **Decide monitoring.** State whether it has a health check and whether it appears on the status page | Service page; [Observability](../operate/status-and-observability.md) |
| 7 | **Review threats and access.** Cover untrusted input, the shared session cookie, secrets and least privilege | [Security, privacy and access](../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md) |
| 8 | **Write deployment and rollback notes.** Say how it is released and how it is reversed | [Environments and deployment model](../platform/governance/environments.md) |
| 9 | **Update documentation and status in the same pull request** | This checklist |

## Steps

1. Open the pull request and describe the justification (requirement 1).
2. Add the catalogue record. Use `planned` until the service is verified as running, and set `evidence` honestly.

   ```json title="Catalogue record (illustrative)"
   {
     "slug": "example",
     "hostname": "example.rjmlaird.co.uk",
     "title": "Example",
     "purpose": "One public-safe sentence",
     "classification": "integration",
     "visibility": "restricted",
     "lifecycle": "planned",
     "evidence": "none",
     "documentation": "catalogue/first-party/example.md",
     "publish": true,
     "status": null,
     "health": null,
     "repository": null
   }
   ```

3. Create the service page. Give it `visibility` and `lifecycle` front matter that match the record, and link to shared pages instead of repeating their rules.
4. Run `pnpm run docs:generate`, then `pnpm run docs:check`, and commit the regenerated table.
5. Add the page to `sidebars.ts` in the right group.
6. Build the site and fix any broken link before requesting review.

## Never include

Secrets, credentials, account or binding identifiers, bucket names, internal hostnames, private management or health URLs, and exact access-policy rules.

## After launch

Change `lifecycle` to `active` only when a repository or a check verifies the service, and update the page, the catalogue and the status page together. To retire a service, set `retired`, redirect or remove DNS in the same change, and record the decision.

The review workflow for publishing a dataset through the public reference-data service, including licence, attribution and withdrawal.

This is the proposed workflow for the [data](../catalogue/first-party/data.md) service. Publishing is a deliberate, reviewed act: nothing reaches the public service automatically.

:::info[Status: Proposed]
No dataset has been published through this workflow yet. Adjust it once the service is deployed.
:::

## Before you start

A dataset is eligible only if all of these hold:

- It is public, or you have the right to publish it
- Its licence permits redistribution, and you can state the licence and the attribution it requires
- It contains no personal, customer or private data
- You can name the source and the date it was retrieved

## Workflow

1. **Record the source.** Note where the data came from, its licence, the required attribution and the retrieval date.
2. **Prepare the data.** Clean it reproducibly, with the steps kept in the repository, and define its schema.
3. **Validate.** Check the data against the schema. Reject unexpected fields and missing required values.
4. **Describe it.** Write the metadata: title, description, source, licence, attribution, coverage, update frequency and version.
5. **Review.** A second look at licence, attribution and personal data before anything is merged.
6. **Publish a version.** Release it as a new, immutable version. Never overwrite a published version in place.
7. **Verify.** Fetch the published response and compare it with the source.
8. **Announce.** Update the dataset catalogue and any affected documentation.

## Changing and withdrawing

- A correction is a new version. Keep the previous one available unless it is wrong in a harmful way.
- A breaking schema change is a new major version; see [APIs and integrations](../platform/architecture/apis-and-integrations.md#contract-and-versioning-rules).
- If a dataset must be withdrawn, for example because of a licence or privacy problem, remove it promptly, record why and tell known consumers.

## Never publish

Personal data, customer records, credentials, anything under a licence that forbids redistribution, or data you cannot attribute. See [Security, privacy and access](../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md#privacy).

How to detect, contain, communicate and learn from an incident affecting the rjmlaird.co.uk estate, written for a single maintainer.

This guide expands the process in [Observability, status and incident response](status-and-observability.md). It is written for one person acting under pressure, so each step says what to do first.

## First ten minutes

1. **Stop the harm.** Roll back a release, disable a route or revoke access. Prefer the quickest reversible action.
2. **Rotate anything exposed.** If a secret may have leaked, rotate it now; see [Secret rotation](runbooks/secret-rotation.md).
3. **Write down what you see.** Time, symptoms and what you changed. You will need this later.
4. **Decide if personal data is involved.** If it may be, treat the incident as serious and go to the section below.

## What kind of incident is it?

| Situation | First action |
| --- | --- |
| Public site down or defaced | Roll back the last deployment; check DNS and hosting |
| Webhook failures or missing payments | Follow [Webhook failures](runbooks/webhook-failures.md) |
| Suspected leaked credential | Rotate it, then review recent use |
| Unexpected access to a restricted service | Revoke the credential or session, then review the access policy |
| Dependency or build compromise | Stop deployments, pin the previous known-good version and review the lockfile |

## Communicate

- If public services are affected, update the [status](../catalogue/first-party/status.md) page once it exists. Say what is affected and when you will next update, not guesses about cause.
- Tell affected customers or partners directly when their data or service is involved.

## Personal data

If personal data may have been lost, exposed or altered, consider your legal duties straight away. Under UK GDPR, a notifiable personal data breach must generally be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. Check the current ICO guidance before relying on this, and seek advice where unsure.

## Review

Within a few days, write a short note:

- What happened, and the timeline
- Impact, and who was told
- Root cause
- What worked, and what slowed you down
- Follow-up actions, each with an owner and a date

If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an [ADR](../platform/decisions/index.md) and update the affected service page.

# Service ownership

Every maintained service should identify a responsible owner or role, a canonical repository, an operational contact route where appropriate, and a review date. If ownership is unknown, state `To confirm`; do not imply that a named individual or team has accepted responsibility.

## Minimum ownership record

- **Accountable owner:** role or team responsible for lifecycle and risk decisions.
- **Technical maintainer:** role responsible for code, configuration and deployment.
- **Documentation reviewer:** owner or delegate who confirms that the page remains accurate.
- **Review cadence:** normally six months for service records, and after material interface, access or deployment changes.
- **Evidence:** repository, deployment evidence or owner confirmation supporting lifecycle claims.

## Review triggers

Review the record when a hostname, owner, data flow, dependency, public interface, security boundary, deployment process or lifecycle changes. Update the canonical registry as part of the same change when it contains the affected fact.

How the health of the ecosystem is monitored, how status is communicated and what to do when something breaks. Mostly proposed; little is confirmed.

Good observability for a small ecosystem means knowing quickly that something is broken, finding out why, and telling the right people. Almost none of that is documented as in place, so this page is mainly a proposal and a list of questions.

:::info[Status: Proposed]
No monitoring, error-tracking, analytics or status tooling is confirmed. Candidate tools below are options to evaluate, not decisions.
:::

## What exists today

| Capability | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Build failure notification for the docs | GitHub Actions run status only |
| Worker logs and metrics | Cloudflare provides these for Workers. The services Workers emit structured JSON logs with request, correlation and event identifiers and redact emails and tokens; where the logs are read is to confirm |
| Uptime monitoring | To confirm |
| Error tracking | To confirm |
| Public status page | Proposed (`status`); no confirmed implementation |
| Analytics | To confirm |

## Proposed approach

### Health checks

Each service should offer one cheap endpoint that returns whether it is healthy. The API template in these docs already sketches `GET /status` returning `ok` and `version`; adopt a consistent form such as `GET /v1/status` across every Worker.

Each catalogue entry says whether a service is public. Only public services may publish a health URL, and restricted services' checks stay private. Never list internal health or monitoring URLs in public documentation.

### Logging

- Log events, not secrets or personal data.
- Include a request or event identifier so a failed webhook can be traced from provider to consumer.
- Keep retention short unless a legal or business reason says otherwise.

### Status communication

Host any public status page **outside** the infrastructure it reports on. A status page that goes down with the thing it monitors tells nobody anything. The page is curated: it reports a service state, drawn from the catalogue's public services, not raw metrics or logs. See [status](../catalogue/first-party/status.md).

### Alerting

Alert on a small number of things you would act on at once: webhook failures, a failed scheduled sync, and the public sites being unreachable. Too many alerts will be ignored.

## Incident response

The full guide is [Incident response](incident-response.md). A pragmatic process for a single maintainer:

1. **Detect.** An alert, a failed workflow run or a report.
2. **Assess.** What is affected, and is any personal data involved?
3. **Contain.** Roll back, disable a route or rotate a secret.
4. **Communicate.** Update the status page if public services are affected. If personal data may have been exposed, consider legal reporting duties promptly.
5. **Fix and verify.**
6. **Review.** Write a short note. If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an [ADR](../platform/decisions/index.md).

## To confirm

1. Is any uptime monitoring running?
2. Are Cloudflare Worker logs enabled, and where are they read?
3. Who is notified when a scheduled job fails?
4. Is there any analytics on the public sites, and if so which?

How rjmlaird.co.uk and its subdomains are resolved, which parts of the DNS setup are confirmed, and the rules for adding or retiring a subdomain.

The domain architecture of rjmlaird.co.uk is intended to keep DNS small, predictable and easy to audit. This page records what is known about the current setup, what is inferred, and the rules that decide whether a new subdomain gets created. :::info[Status: Draft] Only the docs hostname is verified from a repository. The registrar and authoritative nameservers are **not yet documented**. Treat everything marked *inferred* or *To confirm* as unchecked. ::: ## Global DNS strategy | Question | Answer | Basis | | --- | --- | --- | | Who is the registrar? | To confirm | Not recorded | | Who runs the authoritative nameservers? | Probably Cloudflare | **Inferred**: the auth Worker uses a Custom Domain route, which requires the zone's DNS to be managed by Cloudflare | | How does `docs` resolve? | CNAME to GitHub Pages | Repository README and `static/CNAME` | | How do Worker hostnames resolve? | Cloudflare Worker Custom Domains | Owner-stated for `auth` and `hooks` | | Is there a wildcard DNS record? | To confirm | Not recorded | | Is DNSSEC enabled? | To confirm | Not recorded | The practical consequence is a **split hosting model**. Static content may live on GitHub Pages or another static host, while services live on Cloudflare Workers. DNS is the one place that holds the whole picture together, which is why it deserves its own documentation. ## Root domain and apex routing The planning inventory names `www.rjmlaird.co.uk` as the canonical web presence and `rjmlaird.co.uk` as the root domain. **Proposed rule:** pick one canonical host and permanently redirect (301) the other to it. Following the inventory, that means: - `https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk` serves the site. - `https://rjmlaird.co.uk` redirects to `https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk`, preserving the path. **Trade-offs.** Using `www` as canonical is the traditional choice and keeps the apex record simple. Using the apex as canonical gives shorter URLs and matches how the site is already referred to elsewhere. Either works; what matters is choosing one and applying it everywhere, including sitemaps, `rel="canonical"` tags and cookie scope. :::note[To confirm / technical debt] The docs site currently links to the **apex** (`https://rjmlaird.co.uk`) in its navbar and footer, which contradicts the inventory's choice of `www` as canonical. Decide which host is canonical, then update `docusaurus.config.ts` to match. Record the decision in an [ADR](decisions/index.md). ::: ## Subdomain resolution rules 1. **Lowercase, single-label, one purpose.** For example `docs`, never `docs-and-guides`. The domain architecture of rjmlaird.co.uk is intended to keep DNS small, predictable and easy to audit. This page records what is known about the current setup, what is inferred, and the rules that decide whether a new subdomain gets created.

:::info[Status: Draft] Only the docs hostname is verified from a repository. The registrar and authoritative nameservers are not yet documented. Treat everything marked inferred or To confirm as unchecked. :::

Global DNS strategy

QuestionAnswerBasis
Who is the registrar?To confirmNot recorded
Who runs the authoritative nameservers?Probably CloudflareInferred: the auth Worker uses a Custom Domain route, which requires the zone’s DNS to be managed by Cloudflare
How does docs resolve?CNAME to GitHub PagesRepository README and static/CNAME
How do Worker hostnames resolve?Cloudflare Worker Custom DomainsOwner-stated for auth and hooks
Is there a wildcard DNS record?To confirmNot recorded
Is DNSSEC enabled?To confirmNot recorded

The practical consequence is a split hosting model. Static content may live on GitHub Pages or another static host, while services live on Cloudflare Workers. DNS is the one place that holds the whole picture together, which is why it deserves its own documentation.

Root domain and apex routing

The planning inventory names www.rjmlaird.co.uk as the canonical web presence and rjmlaird.co.uk as the root domain.

Proposed rule: pick one canonical host and permanently redirect (301) the other to it. Following the inventory, that means:

  • https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk serves the site.
  • https://rjmlaird.co.uk redirects to https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk, preserving the path.

Trade-offs. Using www as canonical is the traditional choice and keeps the apex record simple. Using the apex as canonical gives shorter URLs and matches how the site is already referred to elsewhere. Either works; what matters is choosing one and applying it everywhere, including sitemaps, rel="canonical" tags and cookie scope.

:::note[To confirm / technical debt] The docs site currently links to the apex (https://rjmlaird.co.uk) in its navbar and footer, which contradicts the inventory’s choice of www as canonical. Decide which host is canonical, then update docusaurus.config.ts to match. Record the decision in an ADR. :::

Subdomain resolution rules

  1. Lowercase, single-label, one purpose. For example docs, never docs-and-guides. Names describe a function, not a vendor.
  2. No subdomain without a catalogue entry. Every record must correspond to a row in the subdomain catalogue with a status and an owner.
  3. No wildcard DNS record. A wildcard hides typos and widens the takeover surface. (The shared session cookie is scoped to *.rjmlaird.co.uk, but that is a cookie setting, not a DNS record.)
  4. Remove records when retiring a service. A CNAME pointing at a deleted GitHub Pages site or an abandoned SaaS tenant can be claimed by someone else. Delete the DNS record in the same change that retires the service.
  5. Prefer redirects to new hostnames. A retired subdomain should redirect to its path replacement for as long as old links are likely to exist, then be removed.

This section documents the architecture behind **rjmlaird.co.uk**: the sites, services and infrastructure that make up Ryan Laird's personal, professional and technical web presence. It is written for four readers: the owner and maintainer, future collaborators and contractors, technical readers who want to see how the pieces fit, and non-technical readers who only need a mental model.

:::warning[Read the status labels]
The subdomain list that this section is built around is a **planning model**, not an inventory of running services. Every site and service carries a status label, and anything not yet checked is marked **To confirm**. If a page does not say something is *Live*, do not assume it is.
:::

## How to read this section

### Status labels

| Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Live** | Serving real traffic today. |
| **In development** | Being built; not yet serving production traffic. |
| **Proposed** | Designed or recommended, but no build has started. |
| **Deferred** | Deliberately postponed until there is a concrete need. Includes exploratory ideas. |
| **Not recommended** | Considered and advised against. Recorded so the question is not reopened by accident. |
| **Deprecated** | Was live; scheduled for removal or already retired. |

### Confidence labels

Each page also carries a `confidence` value in its front matter: **Verified** (checked against a repository or configuration), **Partly verified**, or **Unverified** (from planning notes only). Where a statement is inferred rather than confirmed, it is flagged inline.

## System vision and scope

The ecosystem exists to do five jobs:

1. **Present** a clear professional and personal brand.
2. **Publish** writing, research and astronomy and space communication.
3. **Sell and schedule** services such as tutoring, mentoring and coaching.
4. **Explore** ideas in public through experiments and data pieces.
5. **Run** a small amount of back-office automation behind the scenes.

**In scope:** the public sites, the services and APIs, the documentation site and the infrastructure that connects them.

**Out of scope:** the internals of third-party platforms (GitHub, Stripe, Cal.com, HubSpot, Notion, Zotero). Only the integration points are documented here.

## Guiding principles

1. **Status before subdomain.** Nothing gets a DNS record until it has a catalogue entry with a purpose, a status and an owner.
2. **Paths before subdomains.** Content that shares a build, an audience and a security boundary belongs at a path on the main site. A subdomain must justify itself (see the [subdomain catalogue](governance/subdomains.md#when-a-subdomain-is-justified)).
3. **Static first.** Use a static site wherever possible. Add a Worker only where server-side behaviour is genuinely needed.
4. **Keep public and private surfaces apart.** The public portfolio API and the commercial webhook services are separate systems. Private tools sit behind authentication.
5. **One brand system.** `global.css` on the main site is the single source of truth for the visual identity. Other sites copy from it, never the reverse.
6. **Say what we do not know.** Unknowns are written down as **To confirm**, not papered over.
7. **Prefer reversible, low-cost choices.** This is a one-person operation; every extra moving part is maintenance debt.

## Ecosystem summary

Hostnames, visibility and lifecycle for every service are held in the canonical catalogue and published as the [generated public service catalogue](../catalogue/generated/subdomain-catalogue.md). Each service has a page under [Platform services](../catalogue/first-party/platform-services.md). This section does not repeat them.

## A mental model for non-technical readers

Think of the ecosystem as a shop with four areas:

- **The shop windows** are the public sites: the main site, the docs, the labs and, later, space and research content. Visitors browse them freely.
- **The locked doors** are the sign-in service and the private wiki. Only the owner gets through.
- **The back office** is the set of small services that receive a payment or a booking, record it and update the customer record, without anyone pressing a button.
- **The filing cabinets** are the databases and storage buckets where those services keep their records and files.

## Core technologies

| Technology | Used for | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Astro | Main site (`Layout.astro`, `Head.astro`, `global.css`) | Owner-stated |
| Docusaurus 3.10.2 (React 19, Mermaid, local search) | Documentation site | Repository |
| GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions | Hosting and deployment of the docs | Repository |
| pnpm 10 and Node.js 22 (in CI) | Package management and builds | Repository |
| Cloudflare Workers, Hono, KV, D1, R2, Queues, Access | Services and APIs | Owner-stated across several repositories |
| TypeScript, Zod, Vitest, Wrangler | Service code, validation, tests, deployment | Owner-stated |
| GitHub OAuth, Stripe, Cal.com, HubSpot, Notion, Zotero | Third-party integrations | Owner-stated |

This copies the current docs/ into versioned_docs/version-1.0. Commit the result alongside the release tag. The version dropdown updates automatically.

Style

  • Sentence case headings
  • One idea per page; link rather than repeat
  • Every code block states its language; add a title when it is a file
  • Use admonitions (:::tip, :::warning) sparingly

Architecture pages

Pages under docs/platform/ follow extra rules: a status and confidence in the front matter, To confirm callouts for anything unverified, and ADRs for significant decisions. See Naming conventions and standards.

Services pages

Pages under docs/catalogue/first-party/ follow the same front matter, To confirm callouts and Related pages convention as architecture pages. Runbooks and the launch checklist are operational pages: keep them short, action-first and free of secret values.

# Start here

This documentation is the public technical overview and contributor knowledge base for the RJM Laird digital platform. It covers websites, first-party services, external integrations, APIs, data products, deployment and operations. It distinguishes verified implementation from planned work.

## How this site is organised

| Section | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| [Platform map](./platform-map.md) | Understand the service boundaries and how the main components relate |
| [Terminology](./terminology.md) | Interpret lifecycle, ownership, contract and governance terms consistently |
| [Access and environments](./access-and-environments.md) | Understand contributor access, environments and safe handling of credentials |
| [Platform architecture](../platform/overview.md) | Find cross-cutting patterns, governance and durable decisions |
| [Service catalogue](../catalogue/index.md) | Look up first-party capabilities and external providers |
| [Build](../build/configuration.md) | Find configuration, deployment and implementation guidance |
| [Operate](../operate/launch-readiness.md) | Find ownership, launch checks, incident response and runbooks |
| [Contributing](./contributing.md) | Update documentation and validate changes |

## Status and evidence

A hostname or catalogue entry is not proof that a service is deployed. Check the lifecycle, evidence, confidence and last-reviewed date on the canonical service record. Use `To confirm` for unknown details instead of guessing.

## Versions

The version dropdown distinguishes the unreleased **Next** documentation from frozen releases, where available. Use the current version for the latest maintained guidance.
